description: Test your knowledge of MI10.1-5 | Healthcare-Associated Infections.

cards.text: What is the definition of CAUTI and name 3 major causative agents.
cards.answer: CAUTI (Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection) is a UTI in a patient with a urinary catheter in place for ≥2 days. Major agents: E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Candida, Enterococcus.

tip.tip: CAU-TI = Catheter + UTI. Remember: gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) are most common in UTIs.

cards.text: Which pathogens typically cause CLABSI vs VAP? How do they differ?
cards.answer: CLABSI (bloodstream): CoNS (S. epidermidis), MRSA, Klebsiella, Candida. VAP (pneumonia): Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, MRSA, ESBL-producing Klebsiella. VAP favors respiratory gram-negatives; CLABSI includes more gram-positives and fungi.

tip.tip: CLABSI = **Line** infection (skin flora + fungi), VAP = **Lung** infection (respiratory pathogens). Think P. aeruginosa = water-loving → ventilator circuits.

cards.text: List the 6 links in the chain of HAI transmission.
cards.answer: 1. Infectious agent (MRSA, C. difficile, etc.) 2. Reservoir (colonized patient, HCW hands, environment) 3. Portal of exit (secretions, urine, blood, exudate) 4. Mode of transmission (contact, droplet, airborne, common vehicle) 5. Portal of entry (IV site, catheter, wound, respiratory tract) 6. Susceptible host (ICU, post-surgical, immunocompromised).

tip.tip: Memorize as: **Agent → Reservoir → Exit → Transmission → Entry → Host**. Each link = intervention point.

cards.text: What are the 5 WHO moments for hand hygiene in patient care?
cards.answer: 1. Before patient contact 2. Before aseptic procedure 3. After body fluid exposure 4. After patient contact 5. After touching patient surroundings.

tip.tip: Order: **Before contact → Before procedure → After exposure → After contact → After surroundings**. Covers pre/post patient interactions and protection from exposure.

cards.text: Differentiate contact, droplet, and airborne precautions with one organism example each.
cards.answer: Contact: MRSA, C. difficile (direct/indirect contact; use gloves + gown, single room). Droplet: Influenza, meningococcal (>5 µm droplets, <1 m range; surgical mask required). Airborne: TB, measles, varicella (<5 µm nuclei, sustained suspension; N95 respirator, negative-pressure room).

tip.tip: Contact = **closest** (touch/fomites), Droplet = **medium** (cough/sneeze splash), Airborne = **furthest** (invisible mist, stays airborne). More severe = more precautions needed.

cards.text: What is the typical composition of a Hospital Infection Control Committee, and who chairs it?
cards.answer: Chair: Medical Superintendent. Members: Infection Control Officer (microbiologist), Infection Control Nurse (ICN), representatives from surgery, medicine, nursing, pharmacy, housekeeping, and biomedical waste management. Total: usually 8–12 members.

tip.tip: Key roles: Microbiologist = diagnosis, ICN = surveillance/training, Superintendent = governance. Include all major departments for multidisciplinary oversight.

cards.text: Name the 3 device-related HAIs that are most targetable via bundle care.
cards.answer: CAUTI (Catheter-Associated UTI), CLABSI (Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection), and VAP (Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia). These are bundle-preventable through device management, asepsis, and daily assessment.

tip.tip: Remember **CAC-VAP**: CAUTI, CLABSI, VAP. All three involve invasive devices; prevention = early removal + sterile insertion + maintenance bundles.

cards.text: When should C. difficile infection (CDI) be suspected, and why is it distinct from other HAIs?
cards.answer: CDI is suspected in patients with diarrhea after antibiotic exposure, confirmed by toxin A/B positivity. It is distinct because: (1) transmission is via spores (resistant to alcohol-based sanitizers; require hand washing), (2) antibiotic-induced dysbiosis enables overgrowth, (3) requires contact precautions + dedicated equipment.

tip.tip: CDI = **post-antibiotic** diarrhea. Spores survive hand sanitizer → **soap & water only**. Common risk: broad-spectrum antibiotics (cephalosporins, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones).
